sections.text: A shared reference only lets you read. To change a borrowed value, use a mutable reference: &mut. The variable itself must be declared mut.
The key rule: at any moment you can have either one mutable reference, or any number of shared references, but not both.
This rule stops one part of a program from changing data while another part is reading or changing it, which prevents a whole class of bugs called data races.
A borrow lasts until the last time it's used, not until the end of the block. That's why r2 is allowed after the last use of r.
Think of a whiteboard: many people can read it at once, or one person can write on it, but nobody should read while someone is halfway through writing.

exercise.prompt: Finish double so it doubles the number through the mutable reference (use *n). It should print: 42

quiz.question: How many mutable references to a value can be in use at once?
Can you have a &mut and a & to the same value in use at the same time?
What does the dereference operator * do in *r += 1?
options: Follows the reference to change the value it points to
